title: The page after a form submits
metaTitle: The page after a form submits
excerpt: After a form sends, say what you received, what happens next, and when. Give the person a way back. A generic thank-you leaves them guessing.
alt: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back. The clear product views fit a piece about a confirmation that should be just as plain.
caption: Say what arrived, and what happens next. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a confirmation page include?
faqs.answer: Three facts: what you received, what you will do next, and when. If a person requested a call, say that the request arrived and how scheduling works. If they joined a list, say what the first email contains. Offer one way back to the site, usually the homepage or the work, so the tab is not a dead end.

faqs.question: Is a toast or a line above the form enough?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, for a small action they can undo on the same page, like saving a setting. For a request that ends the task, a dedicated confirmation is clearer. The form should disappear or clearly stop accepting a second submit. Leaving the filled form in place makes people send it twice.

faqs.question: Should the confirmation try to sell something else?
faqs.answer: Only after the reassurance is obvious. A wall of unrelated offers feels like the request vanished into a marketing machine. One relevant next step is plenty: read a specific piece of work, or add the call to a calendar if that is how your process actually works. Match the email they receive to the same facts, in the same words.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Say what you received, what happens next, and when. That is the whole job of a form confirmation page. The person just trusted you with a name, a problem, or a payment. The next screen has to prove the trust landed. A generic thank-you, with no path back and no clock, leaves them wondering if they should try again.

They are in a hurry on this page too. Nielsen Norman Group's research on visits says people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is obvious, and that the first 10 seconds do the heaviest work. On a confirmation, the value is reassurance. Put it in the first lines, in the same voice as the form they just finished.

## What you received

Name the thing. "We have your request for an intro conversation" is a fact. "Thanks!" is a mood. The mood can sit beside the fact. It cannot replace it. Include a detail they recognize from what they typed, when that detail is not sensitive: the address they wrote to, the role they asked about, the plan they chose. Recognition is how they believe the submit worked.

Do not echo secrets back in full on a screen they might be sharing. A password reset, a payment, a health detail: confirm the category of what you received and where the next instruction will appear. "A reset link is on its way to the email you use with us" is enough. The full address may be right. The full payload is not.

If the submit can fail, the failure is not a confirmation. Keep the person on the form, next to the field that needs a fix, with the rest of their answers intact. A cheerful thank-you after a silent error is how leads vanish and how customers pay twice. The button should show a pending state, then either a real confirmation or a real error. Those are different pages in spirit even when they share a layout.

Disable the second click while the request is in flight, and ignore a second submit that arrives anyway. The confirmation should be idempotent in the language too. "We have one request from you" is calmer than a second email that contradicts the first. The engineering and the sentence have to agree.

## What happens next, and when

Write the next step in calendar time or in sequence, whichever you can keep. "You will hear from us within one business day" is a promise you must mean. If you cannot mean it, do not write it. "We read these in the order they arrive, on business days" is honest and still useful. Vague urgency, "someone will be in touch soon," forces them to invent a clock and then resent you for missing it.

Say who will reply if a specific role does. "A person on the studio team writes back" is enough when you are small. Do not invent a department you do not have. Do not say a specialist will call in an hour if the truth is an email tomorrow. The confirmation is a contract in miniature. The rest of the relationship is judged against it.

If they need to do something else, say it once, in a list of one or two items. Check spam if you are sending mail. Have a link ready if the next step is a document. Add the event if a time was actually booked. Do not give them homework to make the page look thorough. Every extra step is a chance they decide the submit did not count.

Match the email, the slack message, or the internal note to the same words. If the page says "intro conversation" and the email says "demo request," they will wonder which one they started. Pick the phrase on the form, repeat it on the confirmation, repeat it in the mail. Consistency here is not a brand exercise. It is how a busy person files the event in their head.

## A path back

The confirmation is a page on your site, with the same header and the same type. Offer a way onward that fits the moment. After a contact form, a link to selected work lets them keep learning while they wait. After a purchase, the path is the order, not the homepage slogan. After a newsletter signup, the path might be the latest essay, if you have one worth their time. One link. Maybe two. A sitemap is not a comfort.

Do not trap them in a modal they cannot bookmark. A full page has a URL they can return to if the tab closes, and it can be read by the same access tools as the rest of the site. If you do confirm in place, above the form, make the change obvious and keep a link to whatever they may need next. The worst version is a small green line that disappears, on a form that still looks submittable.

Say whether they should expect to use this browser tab again. "You can close this page" is a kindness when the next step is email. It tells them they are done. People sit on thank-you screens waiting for a spinner that will never come, because the page did not release them.

If the flow was a booking, the confirmation should carry the time, the length, and the place or the link. A naked "you're scheduled" without the when is how people miss the meeting you both wanted. The details belong on the page and in the mail. They also belong in the human note if you send one.

## What not to pile on

Do not turn the thank-you into a second homepage. A grid of offers, a popup for a different list, a survey about the survey: these shout that the page's job is your metrics, not their certainty. If a next step is genuinely relevant, one sentence and one link, after the facts.

Do not autoplay a video of the founder celebrating them. Do not confetti the screen if the action was serious. A short, still page reads as confidence. A production number reads as uncertainty dressed up. Match the stakes. A waitlist for a small tool can be lighter than a migration request for a store. The structure stays the same either way: received, next, when, a way back.

Watch the tracking on this page. It is a poor place to fire a dozen new tags, and a poor place to ask for a review of an experience that has not happened yet. If you measure the conversion, measure the successful submit, once. A confirmation that is slow because of new scripts undoes the calm you just wrote.

Keep the page out of the index if it is a private endpoint, and keep it from being cached as if it were the form. A person who hits back should see a sensible state, not a second silent submit and not an expired error with no explanation. Test the back button. It is part of the flow.

## The mail, the owner, and the empty hour

Decide who owns the reply before you design the page. The confirmation is a promise that a specific person or a specific inbox will act. If requests currently fall into a shared mailbox nobody watches on Fridays, the page should not say otherwise. Fix the watching, or change the sentence. A beautiful confirmation on top of an unattended inbox is how a studio, or a product, earns a quiet reputation for disappearing.

Send yourself the email the visitor receives, on a phone, in the same hour as the test submit. The subject line should be recognizable, the first lines should repeat the three facts, and the reply address should be a place a human reads. A no-reply address plus a confirmation that says "just reply to this email" is a broken pair. Pick one path and support it.

Note the quiet hours in the copy if they are real. "We read new requests on business days" prevents a Sunday night submit from feeling ignored on Sunday night. You do not need a live chat puppet to cover the gap. You need the page to set a clock you can keep.

## Write it before you style it

Draft the confirmation when you draft the form, in the same document. Founders spend hours on the fields and accept the platform's default thank-you. The default is how the careful form ends in a stranger's voice. Bring the three sentences to the build. The layout can be the article layout you already trust: a heading, a short paragraph, a link.

Read it out loud as the person, not as the company. "I asked for a call. I know you have the request. I know you will write tomorrow. I know I can look at the work while I wait." If you cannot say that, the page is missing a fact. Add the fact. Do not add a synonym for thank you.

On a Hanabi project the confirmation is a real route, in the same header as the site, with those sentences written for the specific form. A contact form and a careers form do not share a paragraph. They might share a layout. The words stay particular because the next step is particular.

Place the form and the confirmation next to each other in the review. Submit a real test, to a real inbox, and read both. Then submit an error and see that you do not get the success page. This is a ten-minute check that prevents a quiet leak of trust.

See [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) for the kind of public page a person can keep reading after they have sent a note. The confirmation should feel like the same studio that made the work, not like a plugin that caught the lead.

A calendar is a stricter version of the same promise. [Calendar embeds and the trust around them](/blog/calendar-embeds-and-the-trust-around-them) is the next piece, because a booking page that hides what the meeting is for creates the doubt a confirmation then has to repair.
